source: Authored against the NCERT Class 9 Social Science textbook 'Understanding Society: India and Beyond, Part 1' (bookCode iest1, 9 chapters). CBSE holds no Class 9 board exam and NCERT's Exemplar series covers only Science and Mathematics, so Class 9 Social Science has no official question source; every question here was written from the chapter text itself, extracted from public/ncert/iest1/*.pdf and read in full before authoring. Draft for teacher review - see data/questions.socialscience9.md for grounding, distractor rationale and flagged uncertainties.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: In the chapter's own words, Social Science is best described as:
options: the study of governments and their laws
the systematic study of human society
the study of the natural world and its laws
the study of past events and their dates
questions.explanation: The chapter defines Social Science as 'the systematic study of human society'. It does not only tell us what happened or where things are located; it explains why events occur and how society, environment, government and economy are connected. Physics, Chemistry and Biology study the natural world; Social Science studies society.
questions.origin: iest1 ch1, opening section, p.1

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which set names the four core disciplines that Social Science draws from in Grades 9-10?
questions.explanation: The chapter names Geography, History, Political Science and Economics as the four core disciplines for Grades 9-10. Sociology, Philosophy, Anthropology and Psychology are named too, but as part of the wider Social Science family that is developed in higher grades.
questions.origin: iest1 ch1, 'Social Science as a Study of Disciplines', p.4

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Panchamahabhutas are the five great elements. Which of these is NOT one of them?
questions.explanation: The five are earth (Prithvi), water (Apah), fire (Agni), air (Vayu) and space (Akasha). Metal belongs to a different five-element scheme and is not among them. The chapter presents the Panchamahabhutas as an early attempt to understand nature as one interconnected system in which human life is embedded.
questions.origin: iest1 ch1, margin note on Panchamahabhutas, p.3

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The expression vasudhaiva kutumbakam means:
options: the ruler's first duty is the people's welfare
questions.explanation: Vasudhaiva kutumbakam means 'the world is one family'. The chapter uses it to show that the interconnectedness of human societies across regions and cultures - what Social Science studies as global interaction - is an old idea in India's knowledge traditions.
questions.origin: iest1 ch1, 'Understanding Society through Time and Traditions', p.3

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Arthashastra, attributed to Kautilya and composed about 2,300 years ago, examined:
options: the treatment of physical and mental ailments
the movement of planets and the prediction of rainfall
administration, economic management, taxation and the duties of rulers
the rules of Sanskrit grammar and poetic metre
questions.explanation: The chapter cites the Arthashastra as evidence that systematic thinking about governance and the economy existed in India long before modern academic disciplines took shape. It dealt with administration, economic management, taxation and what a ruler owed the people.
questions.origin: iest1 ch1, 'Understanding Society through Time and Traditions', p.3

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: A historian studying coins issued by King Samudragupta is using which kind of source?
questions.explanation: Numismatic sources are coins, currency and medals. Their metal content, inscriptions and symbols tell historians about the economy, chronology, rulers, trade and political boundaries. Inscriptions cut into stone or metal are epigraphic, which is a separate category.
questions.origin: iest1 ch1, margin note on Numismatic Source and Fig. 1.8, p.8

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: A Brahmi inscription cut into a stone pillar of the Gupta period is an example of:
questions.explanation: An epigraphic source is a text, decree or record inscribed on a durable material such as stone, metal plates or rock surfaces. Such inscriptions give direct evidence about events, rulers, administration and society. Coins would be numismatic; folklore would be oral tradition.
questions.origin: iest1 ch1, margin note on Epigraphic Source and Fig. 1.6, p.8

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which of these is an archaeological source rather than a literary one?
options: A memoir written by a ruler
A terracotta figurine from the Sindhu-Sarasvati Civilisation
A traveller's account of his journey through India
A revenue document listing land holdings
questions.explanation: Archaeological sources are material remains - monuments, architectural structures, excavated sites, artefacts, sculptures and paintings. Travelogues, revenue documents and memoirs are all listed by the chapter as literary sources, because they are written texts rather than objects.
questions.origin: iest1 ch1, 'History' section and Figs. 1.2-1.5, pp.6-7

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which discipline asks where things are located, why they are found there, and how places near or distant affect one another?
questions.explanation: Those are the questions the chapter puts at the centre of Geography. Geography combines a spatial perspective (location and its significance) with a temporal one (change over time), and views the world as a system of interdependencies.
questions.origin: iest1 ch1, 'Geography', p.5

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The chapter cites the Panchayati Raj system as an example of:
options: the working of India's foreign policy
grassroots democracy that gives citizens a voice in local development planning
the separation of powers between the three organs of government
questions.explanation: Political Science studies how power is distributed and exercised. The chapter uses Panchayati Raj to show that political power lives not only in formal national institutions but in local self-governance, where villagers take part in planning their own development.
questions.origin: iest1 ch1, 'Political Science', p.9

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: According to the chapter, sustainable growth means growth that:
options: raises national income as fast as possible
keeps prices stable in every market
distributes all resources equally among all citizens
meets present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs
questions.explanation: The chapter defines sustainable growth in exactly these words while discussing Economics. Fast growth and stable prices are goals a government may balance, but neither is what sustainability means, which is about not borrowing from the future.
questions.origin: iest1 ch1, 'Economics', p.10

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Assertion: Social Science is not a single subject but a group of related disciplines. Reason: Human society is complex, and no single field of study can fully explain it.
options: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion
Both are true but the reason does not explain the assertion
The assertion is true but the reason is false
questions.explanation: The chapter makes this argument with the drought example: one drought touches crops, farmers' incomes, government relief, migration and traditional coping practices at once. Because no single discipline can see all of that, Social Science has to be a family of disciplines. The reason is precisely why the assertion holds.
questions.origin: iest1 ch1, 'Social Science as a Study of Disciplines', p.4

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The theory of plate tectonics is credited in this chapter to:
questions.explanation: The chapter opens the section on plate tectonics by naming W.J. Morgan as the scientist who gave the theory. It explains how the outermost layer of the Earth is broken into plates that move slowly over the semi-molten layer beneath them.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, 'Plate Tectonics', p.13

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The lithosphere, which is broken into tectonic plates, consists of:
options: the outer core and the mantle
the crust together with the upper part of the mantle
questions.explanation: The Earth has three main layers - crust, mantle and core. The rigid outer shell made of the crust plus the upper mantle is the lithosphere, and it is this shell that is broken into plates. Below it lies the semi-molten asthenosphere, which lets the plates move.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, 'Plate Tectonics' and Fig. 2.1, p.14

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: What makes the tectonic plates move?
options: The rotation of the Earth on its axis
The gravitational pull of the Moon
Ocean currents pressing on the sea floor
questions.explanation: Heat from the core makes molten material in the mantle rise while cooler material sinks. This circulation sets up convection currents that push and pull the plates. The Earth's rotation and the Moon's pull act on the atmosphere and the tides, not on plate movement.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, 'Plate Tectonics', p.15

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Himalaya was formed at which kind of plate boundary?
options: A divergent boundary, where two plates moved apart
A transform boundary, where two plates slid past each other
A boundary where an oceanic plate sank beneath a continental plate
A convergent boundary, where two continental plates collided
questions.explanation: At a convergent boundary the plates move towards each other. When two continental plates collide, neither sinks easily, so the crust is crumpled upward into fold mountains such as the Himalaya. When an oceanic plate meets a continental plate the oceanic plate sinks instead, producing volcanoes and earthquakes rather than fold mountains.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, 'Plate Tectonics', p.15

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is the chapter's example of a feature formed at:
options: a hotspot far from any boundary
questions.explanation: At a divergent boundary the plates move away from each other, magma rises from below into the gap, and new crust is created. Mid-ocean ridges such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge are built this way. No crust is created or destroyed at a transform boundary.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, 'Plate Tectonics', p.15

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The San Andreas Fault in the United States is an example of a boundary where plates:
options: sink one beneath the other and form volcanoes
slide past each other without creating or destroying crust
move towards each other and build fold mountains
move apart and form new crust
questions.explanation: This is a transform boundary. Because the plates only grind past each other sideways, no crust is made or lost, but the sudden slipping releases energy - which is why this kind of boundary is known mainly for earthquakes.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, 'Plate Tectonics', p.15

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The 'Ring of Fire', where most earthquakes and volcanoes occur, lies around the:
questions.explanation: Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur along plate boundaries, and the belt of boundaries encircling the Pacific Ocean is so active that it is called the Ring of Fire. Comparing the plate map with the earthquake and volcano map shows the two patterns matching.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, 'Plate Tectonics' and Figs. 2.3-2.4, pp.16-17

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: What is the essential difference between weathering and erosion?
options: Weathering happens underground, while erosion happens on the surface
Weathering is slow, while erosion is always sudden
Weathering only breaks rock down, while erosion also moves the broken material away
Weathering is caused by water, while erosion is caused by wind
questions.explanation: The chapter is explicit that weathering 'does not involve movement of the broken material, only the breaking down', whereas erosion is the wearing away and carrying of material from one place to another by water, wind, ice or waves. Both can be caused by water, and both are usually slow.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, 'Weathering' and 'Erosion', pp.19-20

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Plant roots growing into cracks in a rock and splitting it apart is an example of:
questions.explanation: Biological weathering is caused by plants, animals or micro-organisms, and root-splitting is the chapter's own example of it. Physical weathering is breakage by temperature change, frost or wind; chemical weathering changes the minerals themselves through reaction with water, air or acids.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, 'Weathering', pp.19-20

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed as an agent of gradation?
questions.explanation: The agents of gradation are running water, glaciers, wind, waves and groundwater - external forces that wear down, transport and deposit material and so level the surface. Earthquakes are an internal force of the Earth; they build and disturb relief rather than smooth it.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, 'Agents of Gradation', pp.21-22

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which landforms does the chapter place in the upper course of a river?
options: Beaches, sand bars and sea cliffs
questions.explanation: In the upper course the gradient is steep and erosion is strong, cutting V-shaped valleys and producing waterfalls and rapids. Oxbow lakes and floodplains belong to the middle course, deltas and levees to the lower course, and beaches and sea cliffs are coastal rather than river landforms.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, 'Running Water', p.22

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: A meander grows larger because the river:
options: erodes the inner bank of a bend and deposits sediment on the outer bank
erodes its bed downward faster than sideways
carries no sediment at all in its middle course
erodes the outer bank of a bend and deposits sediment on the inner bank
questions.explanation: Water moves fastest around the outside of a bend, so it cuts into the outer bank; on the slower inside it drops its load. Repeated over time this lateral erosion and deposition widens each bend into a large loop, and the fertile soil left along the banks is what makes meander country good farmland.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, 'Meander', pp.23-24

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: A delta is formed:
options: where a glacier melts and leaves its load behind
at the mouth of a river, where it deposits sediment on entering a sea, ocean or lake
in the upper course, where hard rock resists erosion
wherever a river bends sharply in its middle course
questions.explanation: At its mouth a river slows down and drops the sediment it has carried from upstream, and over time these deposits build a fan-shaped or triangular area of land. Deltas are highly fertile, support crops such as rice and jute, and are also prone to flooding.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, 'Deltas', p.24

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: A sea stack is formed when:
options: an arch collapses, leaving an isolated pillar of rock standing
waves undercut the base of a coast and leave a steep rock face
a cliff retreats and leaves a flat area behind
sediment is deposited along the shoreline by waves
questions.explanation: The chapter gives the sequence of coastal erosion: waves cut caves into weak rock, caves on opposite sides of a headland meet to form an arch, and when the arch finally collapses the isolated pillar left standing is a stack. A steep rock face is a cliff and the flat surface left as a cliff retreats is a wave-cut platform.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, coastal erosion landforms, p.26

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: A bowl-shaped depression at the head of a glacier is called a:
questions.explanation: A cirque is the bowl-shaped hollow carved at the head of a glacier. An arete is the sharp ridge left between two valleys, a hanging valley is where a smaller glacier joins a larger one, and a fjord is a deep narrow inlet where the sea has flooded a glacial valley.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, 'Glaciers' and Fig. 2.17, p.27

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: When two glaciers meet and their side moraines join in the middle, the result is a:
questions.explanation: Lateral moraines form along the sides of a glacier; when two glaciers merge, two lateral moraines come together in the centre of the combined ice stream as a medial moraine. A terminal moraine marks the furthest point the glacier advanced before melting back.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, moraines and Fig. 2.19, p.28

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Crescent-shaped dunes that form where sand is limited and the wind blows mainly from one direction are called:
questions.explanation: Barchan dunes are crescent-shaped and need limited sand and a single prevailing wind direction. Star dunes, with several arms, form where winds arrive from different directions; longitudinal dunes are long ridges parallel to the prevailing wind; parabolic dunes are U-shaped and often held in place by vegetation.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, 'Wind' - dunes, pp.30-31

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Assertion: Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) cause sudden, destructive floods downstream. Reason: Rising temperatures melt glaciers rapidly, raising the water level of glacial lakes until their natural dams of ice or loose moraine give way.
options: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion
Both are true but the reason does not explain the assertion
The assertion is true but the reason is false
questions.explanation: The chapter describes exactly this chain: rapid melting enlarges the lake, pressure builds on a dam made only of ice or loose moraine, and heavy rain, an earthquake, an avalanche or a landslide can then break it. The stored water is released all at once, which is why a GLOF is sudden rather than gradual.
questions.origin: iest1 ch2, 'GLOFs', p.35

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which gas makes up the largest share of the Earth's atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen at about 78 per cent and oxygen at about 21 per cent are the two primary gases. Argon is under 1 per cent and carbon dioxide only about 0.04 per cent - small proportions, though carbon dioxide matters far more than its share suggests because it traps heat.
questions.origin: iest1 ch3, 'Composition of the Atmosphere' and Fig. 3.2, p.40

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The proportion of water vapour in the atmosphere:
options: varies, generally between 0.1 and 0.4 per cent
is fixed at about 21 per cent
is fixed at about 0.93 per cent
is the same at every altitude
questions.explanation: Unlike the main gases, water vapour is variable - the chapter gives a usual range of 0.1 to 0.4 per cent. It is a small share but it is what makes cloud formation and precipitation possible. The composition of the atmosphere also changes with altitude.
questions.origin: iest1 ch3, 'Composition of the Atmosphere', p.40

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Nearly all weather phenomena such as rainfall, fog and hail occur in the:
questions.explanation: The troposphere, averaging about 12 kilometres in height, holds the air we breathe and most of the water vapour and clouds, so it is where weather happens. The stratosphere above it is largely free of clouds and weather disturbances.
questions.origin: iest1 ch3, 'Structure of the Atmosphere', p.41

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Aeroplanes prefer to fly in the stratosphere because it:
options: is where most meteorites burn up
is free of clouds and other weather disturbances
is the layer closest to the Earth's surface
questions.explanation: The stratosphere extends up to about 50 kilometres and is calm and cloud-free, which makes for a smooth flight. Air density is in fact highest near the surface and falls with altitude, and meteorites burn up higher still, in the mesosphere.
questions.origin: iest1 ch3, 'Structure of the Atmosphere', p.42

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The ozone layer, which filters the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation, lies in the:
questions.explanation: The chapter names the ozone layer as a notable feature of the stratosphere. Because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation, this is also the reason temperature does not simply keep falling with height above the troposphere.
questions.origin: iest1 ch3, 'Structure of the Atmosphere', p.42

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Most meteorites entering from space burn up in the:
questions.explanation: The mesosphere is the third layer, extending to about 80 kilometres, and the chapter notes that most meteorites burn up there. Temperature also decreases with altitude in this layer, as it does in the troposphere.
questions.origin: iest1 ch3, 'Structure of the Atmosphere', p.42

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: In which layer does temperature rise rapidly with increasing altitude?
questions.explanation: In the thermosphere the gas molecules absorb the Sun's X-rays and short-wave ultraviolet radiation, so temperature climbs steeply with height. The chapter warns that temperature decreases with altitude only in the troposphere and the mesosphere - a rule students often over-apply to the whole atmosphere.
questions.origin: iest1 ch3, 'Structure of the Atmosphere' and 'Don't Miss Out', p.42

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The auroras - the northern and southern lights - occur in the:
questions.explanation: The thermosphere is where the auroras occur, and it is also the layer that reflects radio waves back to Earth; the ionosphere is part of it. The aurora appears when charged particles of the solar wind are steered towards the magnetic poles and make atmospheric gases glow.
questions.origin: iest1 ch3, 'Structure of the Atmosphere' and Fig. 3.4, p.42

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Climate, as distinct from weather, refers to conditions averaged over:
options: a large area for an extended period, usually thirty years or more
questions.explanation: Weather is the hour-to-hour and day-to-day state of the atmosphere. Climate is the sum total of weather conditions and variations over a large area for a long period, usually thirty years or more - which is why one unusually cold winter does not change a place's climate.
questions.origin: iest1 ch3, 'Weather and Climate', p.43

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: A wind called a 'westerly' is one that:
options: blows from west to east only in winter
blows only in the western part of a country
questions.explanation: The chapter states the naming rule plainly: winds are named after the direction they blow from, so a westerly comes from the west. Reading it as 'blowing towards the west' reverses every wind name on a map.
questions.origin: iest1 ch3, 'Don't Miss Out' on wind naming, p.45

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: A sea breeze blows:
options: from the land to the sea during the day
from the sea to the land at night
from the land to the sea at night
from the sea to the land during the day
questions.explanation: By afternoon the land is warmer than the sea, so air rises over the land and a low-pressure region forms there; wind then blows in from the sea. At night the land cools faster than the sea and the flow reverses, giving the land breeze.
questions.origin: iest1 ch3, land and sea breeze, Fig. 3.8, p.46

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How many distinct seasons does the India Meteorological Department recognise for India?
questions.explanation: The IMD recognises four seasons - winter, summer or pre-monsoon, monsoon, and post-monsoon. Six is the traditional Indian reckoning of ritus, and Himalayan states additionally experience autumn and spring, but the IMD's official count is four.
questions.origin: iest1 ch3, 'Seasons in India', p.47

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The word 'monsoon' comes from the Arabic word mausim, which means:
questions.explanation: Arab traders coming to India named the seasonal reversal of the wind system after mausim, meaning season. Sailors noticed the reversal early because they depended on it to travel, and the word describes the seasonal switch of wind direction rather than the rain itself.
questions.origin: iest1 ch3, 'Monsoon', p.49

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Why does the south-west monsoon blow from the sea towards the land in summer?
options: The Earth's rotation forces all summer winds inland
Melting Himalayan snow draws moist air northward
The land heats faster than the ocean, creating low pressure over the subcontinent
The ocean heats faster than the land, creating low pressure over the sea
questions.explanation: In summer the Indian landmass warms faster than the surrounding oceans, so a low-pressure area forms over land while the cooler Indian Ocean stays at higher pressure. Since wind always moves from high to low pressure, moist air is drawn in from the sea, bringing most of India's annual rainfall.
questions.origin: iest1 ch3, 'Monsoon', p.49

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The north-east or winter monsoon brings significant rainfall mainly to:
options: Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and parts of Karnataka
questions.explanation: The winter monsoon blows from land to sea and is usually cold and dry. Where it crosses the Bay of Bengal it picks up moisture, so the south-eastern coast - Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and parts of Karnataka - gets rain from it while most of the country stays dry.
questions.origin: iest1 ch3, 'Monsoon', p.52

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: In the 2025 Punjab floods case study, which factor is described as a human-made cause rather than a natural one?
options: Rain falling in Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir
Weak and old river embankments and building too close to the rivers
Very heavy monsoon rainfall over Punjab
questions.explanation: The case study separates the two. Heavy monsoon rain, western disturbances and rain in the upper catchments were natural causes. Weak old embankments (dhusi bandh), houses and farms built too close to the rivers, silting of rivers and dams, and late flood warnings were the human-made ones that made the damage worse.
questions.origin: iest1 ch3, 'Punjab Floods 2025: A Case Study', pp.54-55

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Assertion: High-pressure areas are usually associated with clear and sunny skies. Reason: Air always moves from low-pressure areas to high-pressure areas.
options: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion
Both are true but the reason does not explain the assertion
The assertion is true but the reason is false
questions.explanation: The assertion is correct: cold heavy air sinks in a high-pressure area, and sinking air does not form clouds, so the sky stays clear. The reason reverses the rule - air always moves from high pressure to low pressure, which is what makes wind blow in the first place.
questions.origin: iest1 ch3, 'Atmospheric pressure' and 'Wind', p.45

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which early writing system has still not been deciphered?
questions.explanation: The Harappans used a pictographic script found on seals and pottery, but it has not yet been read, so we cannot hear the Harappans in their own words. Cuneiform and hieroglyphs have both been deciphered, and Brahmi - used from about 400 BCE and formalised under Ashoka - is read as well.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, opening section, p.61

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which was the first hominin to move out of Africa?
questions.explanation: Homo erectus, the maker of handaxes and cleavers, was the first to leave Africa, spreading into Asia and Europe between about 2 and 0.5 million years ago. Homo habilis is known from Africa itself; Homo sapiens evolved in Africa around 300,000 years ago and left much later.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, 'Why Should We Study Early Human History?', p.64

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Homo habilis, the 'handy man' who made chopper stone tools, is associated with which site?
options: Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania and Kenya
questions.explanation: Homo habilis lived in Africa, especially at Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania and Kenya. Bhimbetka and Attirampakkam are Indian sites of much later human occupation, and Mehrgarh is a Neolithic farming village, not a site of early hominin fossils.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, 'Who Were Our Human Ancestors?' and Fig. 4.6, p.66

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Attirampakkam, dated to about 1.5-1.7 million years ago, is in which present-day state?
questions.explanation: Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu and Isampur in Karnataka (about 1.2 million years old) are the chapter's two dated examples of very early occupation in the subcontinent, where handaxes, cleavers, scrapers and choppers of quartzite and limestone were found alongside animal fossils.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, 'Palaeolithic Hunter-Gatherers', p.68

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Very small stone tools called microliths are characteristic of which period?
questions.explanation: Microlithic tools mark the Mesolithic, the transitional phase between hunting-gathering and agriculture. The Lower Palaeolithic is known for large tools such as handaxes and cleavers; the Neolithic for polished stone tools; the Chalcolithic for copper used alongside stone.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, Fig. 4.7 and 'Mesolithic Hunter-Gatherers', pp.67, 70

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh, a World Heritage Site, is known for:
options: the earliest evidence of ploughed fields
the oldest agricultural village in the subcontinent
hundreds of painted rock shelters with Mesolithic and earlier occupation
questions.explanation: Bhimbetka preserves hundreds of painted rock shelters used in the Mesolithic and earlier. The ploughed field is at Kalibangan, the oldest farming village is Mehrgarh, and the dockyard is at Lothal - all Harappan or Neolithic sites of a much later date.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, 'Mesolithic Hunter-Gatherers', p.70

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: What was the hallmark of the Neolithic revolution?
options: The domestication of selected plants and animals
The first use of stone tools
questions.explanation: The chapter identifies domestication - bringing selected plants and animals under human control and breeding them - as the hallmark of the Neolithic revolution. Stone tools are far older, writing came with the Bronze Age, and iron smelting belongs to the Iron Age.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, 'The Neolithic Revolution', p.71

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The oldest Neolithic site and earliest agricultural village of the Indian subcontinent, dating to about 7000 BCE, is:
questions.explanation: Mehrgarh, on the Bolan river in present-day Pakistan, dates to about 7000 BCE. Its people built sun-dried brick houses and granaries, cultivated wheat and barley, raised sheep, goats and zebu cattle, and were the first here to make copper objects, entering the Chalcolithic by about 4000 BCE.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, 'Neolithic Period in Indian Subcontinent', p.73

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The ploughed field at Kalibangan, showing horizontal and vertical furrows, is evidence of:
options: double crop cultivation, like today's Rabi and Kharif seasons
the earliest use of iron ploughshares
questions.explanation: Furrows running in two directions across the same field show that two crops were grown, a practice close to the Rabi and Kharif cycle followed even now. The chapter offers it as an example of an agricultural tradition nearly 5,000 years old.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, 'Don't Miss Out' on Kalibangan, Fig. 4.19, p.76

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which set correctly pairs each of the four earliest civilisations with its river system?
options: Harappan - Sarasvati; Mesopotamian - Huang He; Egyptian - Nile; Chinese - Tigris
Harappan - Sindhu and Sarasvati; Mesopotamian - Euphrates and Tigris; Egyptian - Nile; Chinese - Huang He
Harappan - Ganga; Mesopotamian - Nile; Egyptian - Tigris; Chinese - Yangtze
Harappan - Sindhu; Mesopotamian - Nile; Egyptian - Euphrates; Chinese - Huang He
questions.explanation: All four early civilisations grew in fertile river plains: the Harappan along the Sindhu and Sarasvati, the Mesopotamian between the Euphrates and Tigris, the Egyptian along the Nile, and the Chinese in the Huang He basin. Mixing up which river belongs to which is the commonest error here.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, 'Bronze Age Civilisations Outside India', p.77

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The name 'Mesopotamia' is Greek for:
questions.explanation: Mesopotamia means 'the land in between' - the land drained by the Euphrates and Tigris in West Asia, covering mainly modern Iraq and Kuwait with parts of Turkey and south-western Iran. 'The black' (kemet) was what the Egyptians called their own land, after its dark river soil.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, 'Mesopotamian Civilisation', p.77

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Cuneiform, the Sumerian writing system begun around 3200 BCE, was written by:
options: pressing a wedge-shaped stylus into damp clay tablets
carving symbols into animal bones and tortoise shells
painting signs on sheets made from a plant
questions.explanation: Cuneiform takes its name from the Latin cuneus, 'wedge', after the wedge-shaped marks pressed into soft clay. Oracle bones were the Chinese source, papyrus sheets the Egyptian one, and stamped seals are Harappan - each civilisation's material shaped the look of its script.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, 'The Beginning of Writing', pp.80-81

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Our 60-minute hour and 360-degree circle come from the number system of the:
questions.explanation: The Sumerian number system was based on 60, which is why we still count sixty seconds to a minute, sixty minutes to an hour and 360 degrees to a circle. The Sumerians also invented the wheeled cart and the sailboat.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, 'Don't Miss Out' after 'The Beginning of Writing', p.81

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: In Akkadian records of trade, Meluhha is generally identified with:
questions.explanation: The cuneiform tablets of the Akkadian king Sargon name three eastern trading partners: Dilmun (today's Bahrain), Magan (the Oman peninsula) and Meluhha, which is generally taken to be the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation. With the Harappans they traded semi-precious stone beads, ivory, timber, gold dust and probably copper.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, 'The Akkadians' and Fig. 4.26, p.82

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Code of Hammurabi, a compilation of rules for civil and social conduct, belongs to which Mesopotamian power?
questions.explanation: Hammurabi came to power in Babylonia in 1792 BCE and turned a small city-state into an empire. His compilation of rules, the Code of Hammurabi, was applied across that empire and became a model for many later legal systems.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, 'The Babylonians', p.83

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which sequence gives the four Mesopotamian city-based powers in the order the chapter presents them?
questions.explanation: The Sumerians were first to become city-based; the Akkadians overshadowed them in 2334 BCE; Assur took supremacy from the Akkadians around 2154 BCE; and Babylonia rose in central Mesopotamia from 1900 BCE. Hammurabi's fame often makes students place Babylonia earlier than it belongs.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, Fig. 4.22 timeline and 'The Sumerians' to 'The Babylonians', pp.78-83

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Rosetta Stone was the key to reading Egyptian hieroglyphs because it:
options: was written in an early form of Arabic
contained a picture dictionary of hieroglyphic signs
carried the same matter in three kinds of writing, one of which was Greek
listed the names of every pharaoh in order
questions.explanation: Found by Pierre Bouchard in 1799, the stone bore three types of writing including Greek, which people could still read - in effect a bilingual dictionary for a lost language. Jean-Francois Champollion used it to decipher the script in 1822.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, 'Don't Miss Out' on the Egyptian script, p.84

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The name 'China' probably comes from which dynasty?
questions.explanation: The Qin, an Iron Age dynasty and the first imperial dynasty, is credited with unifying the country and probably gave China its name. The Shang and Zhou were the Bronze Age dynasties; the Han, which followed the Qin, is the period when silk became a major export and the route it travelled came to be called the Silk Route.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, 'The Chinese Civilisation', p.89

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Assertion: The four earliest world civilisations all emerged in river plains. Reason: The Harappan script has not yet been deciphered.
options: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion
Both are true but the reason does not explain the assertion
The assertion is true but the reason is false
questions.explanation: Both statements are true - the Harappan, Mesopotamian, Egyptian and Chinese civilisations all grew in fertile river plains, and the Harappan script is still unread. But the undeciphered script has nothing to do with why civilisations arose beside rivers; the real reason is that river plains yielded the agricultural surplus that cities need.
questions.origin: iest1 ch4, 'Bronze Age Civilisations Outside India' and opening section, pp.61, 77

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How many hymns (suktas) does the Rigveda contain?
questions.explanation: The Rigveda is the earliest Veda and contains 1,028 hymns, some praising deities and others reflecting on creation, birth and death. It is also the earliest surviving corpus of Indian literature, which matters because the Harappan script cannot be read.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'The Four Vedas', p.99

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which part of a Veda contains philosophical speculation on the Self (Atman) and the Ultimate Universal Being?
questions.explanation: Each Veda has four parts. The Samhitas are hymns for invoking deities, the Brahmanas explain ritual performance in prose, the Aranyakas expand on the speculations of forest sages, and the Upanishads deal with the Self and the Ultimate Universal Being.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'The Four Vedas', p.99

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which Vedic assembly was a smaller body of select elites that primarily served a judicial function?
questions.explanation: The sabha was the smaller body composed of select elites and mainly judicial. The samiti was the larger assembly dealing with policy decisions and political affairs, and the vidhata was a popular gathering of the janas that discussed warfare and other matters.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'Assemblies during Vedic Period', p.101

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The word janapada literally indicates:
options: a tax paid to the raja
a group of families sharing one gotra
the land where a people (jana) first set its feet - a territorial identity
questions.explanation: Janapada marks the shift from identity based on kinship to identity based on land, a transition placed roughly between 1000 BCE and 600 BCE. Once land mattered, control over agriculture and trade routes mattered too, and administration grew more complex.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'Early Kingdoms and Republics', p.103

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Among the sixteen mahajanapadas, which gradually emerged as the most powerful?
questions.explanation: Magadha, in present-day Bihar, had a strategic location, fertile plains and strong rulers, and expanded over its neighbours. That expansion led on to the Mauryan Empire, one of the largest in early Indian history.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'Early Kingdoms and Republics', p.103

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The royal emblem of the Cholas, the Cheras and the Pandyas respectively were:
options: the tiger, the bow and the fish
the fish, the tiger and the bow
the bow, the fish and the tiger
the lion, the bow and the fish
questions.explanation: The tiger stood for the Cholas, the bow for the Cheras and the fish for the Pandyas. These three, the crowned kings or Vendar of Tamilakam, are known mainly from Sangam literature, dated between 300 BCE and 300 CE.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'Let's Recall' on southern kingdoms, p.105

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the seven constituents (Saptanga) of the state described by Kautilya?
questions.explanation: Kautilya's seven constituents are the king (swami), the ministers and high officials (amatya), the territory with its people (janapada), the fortified towns (durga), the treasury (kosha), the forces of defence and order (danda) and the allies (mitra). Guilds were important economic bodies but are not part of the Saptanga.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'Council of Ministers' and the Saptanga panel, pp.108-109

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Junagadh Rock Inscription near Girnar is unusual because it carries records of:
options: the entire Code of Hammurabi in Sanskrit
three rulers from different periods - Ashoka, Rudradaman I and Skandagupta
a single ruler written in three different scripts
the earliest known Tamil village assembly
questions.explanation: The same rock bears Ashoka's Prakrit edicts on Dhamma from the third century BCE, Rudradaman I's Sanskrit inscription of about 150 CE, and Skandagupta's record from the fifth century CE - roughly 700 years of administration and public works on one surface.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'Don't Miss Out' on Junagadh, Fig. 5.5, p.110

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The dam on Sudarshana Lake near Girnar was built by Pushyagupta, a governor appointed by:
questions.explanation: The Junagadh inscription records that Pushyagupta, Chandragupta Maurya's governor, built the dam. Rudradaman I later repaired the lake and Skandagupta restored it after severe damage, which is how one rock came to hold three dynasties' records.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'Irrigation', pp.128-129

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which new office was introduced in the administration during the Gupta period?
options: The sandhivigrahika, or minister of peace and war
questions.explanation: The Guptas kept most of the earlier administrative structure - mantri, commander-in-chief, amatyas - but added the sandhivigrahika, the minister of peace and war. The gramika and pradeshika belong to the earlier Satavahana-era arrangements described in the same section.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'How Were Empires Administered?', p.112

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Kudavolai or 'ballot pot' system of village elections is described in which inscription?
options: The Uttaramerur inscription of Parantaka I
questions.explanation: The tenth-century Uttaramerur inscription of the Chola king Parantaka I, in Kanchipuram district, describes how names of eligible candidates were written on palm leaves, placed in a pot, and drawn out by a young child in full public view. The elected members were then put into committees called variyams.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'Don't Miss Out' on Uttaramerur, p.115

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Tax-free land grants made to Brahmin settlements by the Chalukyas of Badami were known as:
questions.explanation: The Chalukyas called such grants agraharams, and some of them - at Aihole and Badami - grew into important centres of learning. Brahmadeya was the equivalent term used by the Pallavas; valanadu and bhukti are administrative divisions, not grants.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'How Were Empires Administered?', pp.113-114

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The 'tripartite struggle' for control of Kannauj involved which three powers?
options: The Guptas, the Vakatakas and the Maitrakas
The Cholas, the Cheras and the Pandyas
The Mauryas, the Shungas and the Satavahanas
The Gurjara-Pratiharas, the Palas and the Rashtrakutas
questions.explanation: Kannauj, the Gurjara-Pratihara capital in modern Uttar Pradesh, was contested by three major powers - the Gurjara-Pratiharas, the Palas and the Rashtrakutas - which is why the contest is called tripartite. All three ran the same kind of administration: monarchy at the top with decentralised provinces, districts and villages.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'How Were Empires Administered?', p.114

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The earliest reference to the four social categories understood as varna appears in:
options: the Purushasukta, a hymn in Book 10 of the Rigveda
questions.explanation: The Purushasukta in Book 10 of the Rigveda carries the earliest such reference. The chapter stresses that early Vedic texts show no social status fixed by birth, and quotes Rigveda 9.112.3, where one family holds three different occupations, as evidence of that flexibility.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'Varna and Jati', p.119

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: What is one clear difference between varna and jati as described in the chapter?
options: Jatis were fixed at four while varnas kept multiplying
Only jatis were connected to occupation
The number of varnas was fixed at four, while there was no restriction on the number of jatis
Varnas were regional while jatis were national
questions.explanation: Varnas were always four; jatis were not limited in number and kept growing as new social groups and occupations appeared. Jati emerged from several factors, including intermarriage among varnas, migrating communities becoming endogamous, and territorial differences.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'Varna and Jati', pp.119-120

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which is the correct order of the four ashramas?
questions.explanation: The four stages run in order of life: studentship (brahmacharya), the householder (grihastha), life in the forest (vanaprastha) and renunciation (samnyasa). The last two carry the renunciatory sense that the chapter connects to the later shramana traditions.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'Family and Society' and Fig. 5.8, p.121

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four purusharthas, the goals of life?
questions.explanation: The four purusharthas are dharma (righteousness), artha (material well-being), kama (fulfilment of desires) and moksha (liberation). A yajna is a ritual offering, not a goal of life. The chapter adds that artha is desirable only when guided by dharma.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'Family and Society', p.122

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Alvars and the Nayanmars, saint-poets of the sixth-century Tamil region, composed hymns in praise of:
questions.explanation: The twelve Alvars sang of Vishnu and the sixty-three Nayanmars of Shiva. Together they created the great body of Tamil Bhakti literature, offering a direct connection with the divine that needed no elaborate ritual and was open to all regardless of class or gender.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'Religious Life and the Emergence of Bhakti', p.124

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Nashik cave inscription of the second century CE is cited as evidence that guilds (shrenis):
options: were open only to members of a single jati
acted as banking and credit institutions, paying fixed interest on deposits
controlled the appointment of village headmen
collected land revenue on behalf of the king
questions.explanation: The inscription records money deposited with guilds that were obliged to pay a fixed rate of interest, the income being used to maintain Buddhist monasteries and caves. So guilds were not only associations of traders and artisans but also trusted financial institutions.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'Don't Miss Out' - Guilds as Financial Institutions, p.132

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The basic Mauryan tax on land was generally:
options: a fixed amount of silver coins per household
collected only in years of good harvest
a fixed proportion of the produce, usually one-sixth
questions.explanation: The land tax was a fixed share of the produce, generally one-sixth, and land was classified into categories for assessment. Kautilya describes cultivated land, wasteland or fallow, high and dry land, sown fields and groves - detail that shows how carefully revenue was organised.
questions.origin: iest1 ch5, 'Agriculture and Land Revenue', p.128

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Constitution of India was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on:
questions.explanation: Adoption and commencement are two different dates: the Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949, and it came into force on 26 January 1950. India became independent earlier, on 15 August 1947, before the Constitution existed.
questions.origin: iest1 ch6, opening section, p.137

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How long did the Constituent Assembly, formed in 1946, take to draft the Constitution?
questions.explanation: The Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days to produce the world's longest written Constitution. Its debates drew both on India's own traditions of collective decision-making and on democratic ideas from around the world.
questions.origin: iest1 ch6, 'Tracing Democratic Traditions from Early Times', pp.139-140

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Universal Adult Franchise in India means that:
options: every adult must vote in every election
voting rights depend on education and property
every citizen aged 18 and above has the right to vote by secret ballot
every adult may stand for election to Parliament
questions.explanation: Universal Adult Franchise is the right of every citizen aged 18 and above to vote through a secret ballot, without any test of property, education, caste or sex. It is the practical form popular sovereignty takes - the state drawing its authority from the people.
questions.origin: iest1 ch6, 'Popular Sovereignty', p.140

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which Article provides for amendments to the Constitution, keeping it flexible and responsive?
questions.explanation: Article 368 provides for amendment. The Constituent Assembly's debates show the members wanted a dynamic document that could evolve through lawful amendment without losing its fundamental values. Article 32 is the right to constitutional remedies, 21A the right to education, and 46 concerns weaker sections.
questions.origin: iest1 ch6, 'Tracing Democratic Traditions from Early Times', p.140

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How many Fundamental Rights are enshrined in the Indian Constitution?
questions.explanation: There are six: the Right to Equality, the Right to Freedom, the Right Against Exploitation, the Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and the Right to Constitutional Remedies. Eleven is the number of Fundamental Duties, which is a different list.
questions.origin: iest1 ch6, 'Fundamental Rights', p.141

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which right allows a citizen to move the Supreme Court directly when a Fundamental Right is violated?
questions.explanation: The Right to Constitutional Remedies under Article 32 is what makes the other rights enforceable - a right with no way to enforce it would be only a promise. Citizens may also approach a High Court under Article 226.
questions.origin: iest1 ch6, 'Fundamental Rights', p.141

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Right to Education, added as Article 21A in 2009, guarantees free and compulsory education for children aged:
questions.explanation: Article 21A covers children from 6 to 14 years. It was added in 2009, which is why the chapter presents it as an example of the Constitution growing through amendment rather than standing still.
questions.origin: iest1 ch6, 'Let's Explore' after Fundamental Rights, p.141

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Under the separation of powers, the judiciary's distinct role is to:
questions.explanation: The legislature makes laws, the executive implements them and the judiciary interprets them. Keeping these apart prevents power concentrating in one organ: Parliament may amend the Constitution, but the judiciary can review whether an amendment or a law is consistent with it.
questions.origin: iest1 ch6, 'Separation of Powers', p.142

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which country does the chapter give as its example of a direct democracy?
questions.explanation: Switzerland is the example of direct democracy, where citizens take part in most decision-making themselves. India and Canada are parliamentary representative democracies and the USA is a presidential one; direct democracy is described as difficult to run in large countries.
questions.origin: iest1 ch6, Fig. 6.4 'Types of Democracy', p.146

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: In the comparison of democracies, which country is listed as having an unwritten constitution?
questions.explanation: The United Kingdom is a parliamentary democracy with a constitutional monarchy and an unwritten constitution. India, Switzerland and the USA all have written constitutions - a point worth noticing, since a country can be democratic without a single written document.
questions.origin: iest1 ch6, comparison table of democracies, p.148

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The PESA Act of 1996 applies to tribal areas and empowers:
options: Autonomous District Councils in the north-eastern states
the district collector to approve all village spending
the Gram Sabha as the primary decision-making body
the state Governor to nominate village heads
questions.explanation: PESA - the Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas Act - makes the Gram Sabha the primary decision-making body in scheduled tribal areas outside the north-east. Autonomous District Councils are the separate arrangement for specific north-eastern regions.
questions.origin: iest1 ch6, 'Democracy in Practice: India's Living Democracy', p.151

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Article 243(d) of the Constitution provides for women in every Panchayat:
options: not less than one-third reservation of seats filled by direct election
exactly 50 per cent reservation of all seats
reservation only in the post of Sarpanch
no reservation, leaving it to each state
questions.explanation: The constitutional floor is not less than one-third. Many states have gone further on their own - 21 states and 2 Union Territories provide 50 per cent reservation for women in Panchayati Raj Institutions - but 50 per cent is a state provision, not the constitutional minimum.
questions.origin: iest1 ch6, 'Women's Reservation in Local Bodies', p.153

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How did women in India obtain the right to vote, compared with Britain and the United States?
options: Only after a long protest movement lasting into the 1960s
Earlier than in Britain but later than in the United States
Only in states that chose to grant it
It came with the Constitution in 1950 for all citizens at once, without a prolonged separate struggle
questions.explanation: Britain gave women full voting rights in 1928 and the United States in 1920, both after decades of protest. In India, Universal Adult Franchise was extended to men and women together when the Constitution came into force in 1950. The chapter adds that the right to vote does not by itself ensure equal participation.
questions.origin: iest1 ch6, 'Women and the Right to Vote: The Indian Experience', p.153

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The National Emergency of 1975-77 was imposed on the ground of:
options: the failure of constitutional machinery in a state
external aggression by a neighbouring country
questions.explanation: The Emergency was declared in June 1975 on the ground of internal disturbance. Most Fundamental Rights were suspended, the press was censored and many leaders were arrested. It was lifted in 1977, and the ruling government's defeat in the elections that followed is presented as a demonstration of the system's resilience.
questions.origin: iest1 ch6, 'Emergency', pp.155-156

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Right to Information Act, which lets citizens seek information from government departments, came into force in:
questions.explanation: The RTI Act came into force in 2005 after being debated in Parliament and refined through consultation. The chapter uses it as an example of accountability and transparency being built through ordinary democratic processes rather than imposed from outside.
questions.origin: iest1 ch6, 'Accountability and Transparency' and the RTI box, pp.143, 154

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Assertion: India is described as the world's largest democracy. Reason: In 2024 it had a voter base of over 96.8 crore, the largest anywhere.
options: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion
Both are true but the reason does not explain the assertion
The assertion is true but the reason is false
questions.explanation: The chapter ties the title directly to the scale of participation - a population of over 140 crore and more than 96.8 crore registered voters in 2024. It also notes that the word 'largest' refers to numbers, and that challenges of deeper inclusion and representation remain.
questions.origin: iest1 ch6, 'Let's Recall' opening and 'Don't Miss Out', pp.137, 149

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which of these is filled through direct election?
questions.explanation: Members of the Lok Sabha, the Vidhan Sabha and local bodies are chosen directly by voters every five years. The President, the Vice President and members of the Rajya Sabha are elected indirectly, by representatives whom the people have already elected.
questions.origin: iest1 ch7, 'Why do Elections Matter?', p.161

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Psephology, from the Greek psephos meaning 'pebble', is:
options: the study of political parties' finances
the counting of votes by hand
questions.explanation: Psephology is the scientific study of elections. The name recalls ancient Greece, where pebbles were used for voting - psephos plus logy, 'systematic study'. Redrawing constituency boundaries is delimitation, a different process.
questions.origin: iest1 ch7, 'Don't Miss Out' on psephology, p.162

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Members of the Lok Sabha and the Vidhan Sabha are elected using:
questions.explanation: The framers of the Constitution discussed the main electoral systems and chose the plurality or First-Past-The-Post system for the Lok Sabha and the Vidhan Sabha. Proportional representation with a single transferable vote is used for the Rajya Sabha, the Vidhan Parishad, and the President and Vice President.
questions.origin: iest1 ch7, 'The Electoral System', p.163

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Under the First-Past-The-Post system, a candidate wins when they:
options: win a share of seats matching their party's share of votes
survive a second round of voting against the runner-up
receive the most votes, even if that is less than 50 per cent of votes polled
receive more than 50 per cent of the votes polled
questions.explanation: FPTP asks only who is ahead, not whether the winner crossed half the votes. The chapter contrasts it with a majority system, where a candidate must cross 50 per cent or face the runner-up in a second round, and with proportional representation, where seats follow each party's vote share.
questions.origin: iest1 ch7, 'Electoral Systems' comparison table, p.164

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How many Indian states have a bicameral legislature with both a Vidhan Sabha and a Vidhan Parishad?
questions.explanation: Six states have two houses: Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh. Their Vidhan Parishad members are elected by proportional representation with a single transferable vote, with some nominated by the Governor.
questions.origin: iest1 ch7, 'The Electoral System', p.163

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Representation of the People Act, 1950 deals mainly with:
options: nomination of candidates, campaigns and post-election disputes
the election of the President and the Vice President
the recognition of national and state political parties
allocation of seats, delimitation of constituencies and preparation of electoral rolls
questions.explanation: The 1950 Act covers seats, constituency boundaries, electoral rolls and the right of every citizen of 18 and above to vote. The 1951 Act covers the actual conduct of elections - nominations, campaigns, voting procedures, disputes and corrupt practices. Presidential elections have their own Act of 1952.
questions.origin: iest1 ch7, 'The Laws', p.165

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Delimitation is the process of:
options: deciding the dates on which polling will be held
fixing the number of seats and the territorial boundaries of constituencies
removing ineligible names from the electoral roll
allotting election symbols to political parties
questions.explanation: Delimitation fixes how many seats a state has and where the boundaries lie, so that the ratio of seats to population is as equal as possible. Without it one MP might represent five lakh people and another twenty-five lakh, which would defeat equal representation.
questions.origin: iest1 ch7, 'Delimitation Commission', p.166

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution mandates the establishment of a Delimitation Commission?
questions.explanation: Article 82 mandates the Delimitation Commission; India has had four, in 1952, 1963, 1973 and 2002. Articles 324 to 329 provide for the Election Commission, which is a separate body with a permanent role.
questions.origin: iest1 ch7, 'Don't Miss Out' on Article 82, p.166

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Election Commission of India was established on:
questions.explanation: The ECI was established on 25 January 1950, a day before the Constitution came into force - which is why 25 January is observed as National Voters' Day. It is an autonomous permanent constitutional body.
questions.origin: iest1 ch7, 'Let's Recall' on the ECI and the National Voters' Day box, pp.167, 169

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which Articles of the Constitution provide for the Election Commission of India and define its powers?
questions.explanation: Articles 324 to 329 establish the ECI and set out its powers and duties, vesting in it the superintendence, direction and control of the whole election process. Articles 352 to 360 deal with emergencies, and Articles 14 to 18 with the Right to Equality.
questions.origin: iest1 ch7, 'Let's Recall' on the ECI, p.167

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) conducted by the ECI is meant to:
options: review the election symbols allotted to parties
update, verify and correct the electoral rolls so no eligible voter is left out and no ineligible one included
recount votes after a disputed result
questions.explanation: SIR updates and verifies the rolls: it adds voters who have just turned 18 and may not know how to register, and deletes names on grounds of death, change of residence, duplicate enrolment or being permanently untraceable. Claims and objections are settled before the final roll is published.
questions.origin: iest1 ch7, 'ECI creates the electoral roll', pp.167-168

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which app allows a voter to report violations of the Model Code of Conduct within minutes of witnessing them?
questions.explanation: cVIGIL lets voters report violations and election misconduct, with flying squads navigating to the spot using the auto-location. Suvidha is for candidates and parties seeking permissions, Saksham is for persons with disabilities, and Sugam manages vehicles on election duty.
questions.origin: iest1 ch7, Fig. 7.6 digital ecosystem, p.170

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Electronically Transmitted Postal Ballot System (ETPBS) was developed for:
options: service voters posted outside their own constituency
senior citizens above 85 years of age
voters with a benchmark disability of 40 per cent
questions.explanation: ETPBS lets service voters receive a postal ballot electronically and cast it from wherever they are posted, outside their assigned constituency. Home voting is the separate facility offered to senior citizens above 85 and to persons with disabilities of 40 per cent benchmark disability.
questions.origin: iest1 ch7, 'Let's Explore' on ETPBS and Fig. 7.6, pp.168, 170

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Voting from home was extended across India for the first time in the 2024 General Elections for senior citizens above:
questions.explanation: The facility covers senior citizens above 85 and persons with disabilities with a benchmark disability of 40 per cent. It is one of several steps aimed at accessibility, alongside EVMs with Braille and assistance at polling stations.
questions.origin: iest1 ch7, 'Ensuring free and fair elections', p.169

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Anti-Defection Law was passed in 1985 through the:
questions.explanation: The 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1985 brought in the Anti-Defection Law to give elected governments stability. A member who voluntarily gives up party membership or votes against the party whip can be disqualified, and the Speaker or Chairman of the House decides such cases.
questions.origin: iest1 ch7, 'Don't Miss Out' on the Anti-Defection Law, p.175

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Under the criteria for recognition, a party is recognised as a national party if, among other conditions, it:
options: has been registered with the ECI for at least ten years
is recognised as a State Party in at least four states
contests elections in at least two states
wins at least one seat in the Lok Sabha
questions.explanation: Any one of three conditions suffices for national recognition: 6 per cent of valid votes in four or more states plus four Lok Sabha seats; or at least 2 per cent of Lok Sabha seats with candidates elected from at least three states; or recognition as a State Party in at least four states. Simply contesting widely or winning one seat is not enough.
questions.origin: iest1 ch7, Fig. 7.12 criteria for party recognition, p.176

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Opportunity cost is:
options: the money actually paid for a good
the profit earned from a chosen option
the tax paid on a purchase
the value of the alternative that is given up when a choice is made
questions.explanation: When one alternative is chosen the others are given up, and the value of what is given up is the opportunity cost. It is not the price on the bill: a farmer who grows more barley pays for it in the wheat that is no longer grown.
questions.origin: iest1 ch8, 'Choices and Limited Resources', p.184

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The word 'Economics' comes from the Greek oikonomia, which means:
questions.explanation: Oikonomia combines oikos, household, and nemein, management. The chapter uses the origin to make a point: the same problem of getting the most out of limited means faces a family and a nation alike.
questions.origin: iest1 ch8, 'What does Economics Deal with?', p.186

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Production Possibility Curve shows:
options: the different combinations of goods that can be produced using all available resources
the prices at which goods will be sold in a market
the quantity consumers are willing to buy at each price
how national income grows over the years
questions.explanation: The PPC plots the combinations a producer can achieve when resources are fully and efficiently used, with no wastage. Because it slopes downward, moving along it towards more barley always means less wheat - the curve is a picture of opportunity cost.
questions.origin: iest1 ch8, 'Choices and Limited Resources' and Fig. 8.3, p.185

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the factors of production named in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The factors of production are land, labour, capital and technology. Opportunity cost is not an input at all - it is the value of the alternative sacrificed when a producer decides how to combine those inputs.
questions.origin: iest1 ch8, 'How to Produce?' and Fig. 8.6, pp.189-190

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The three key questions that every economy must answer are:
options: What to import, what to export, and what to store
What to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce
What to buy, when to buy, and at what price
How much to tax, how much to spend, and how much to save
questions.explanation: These three questions follow from the mismatch between unlimited wants and limited resources. What to produce settles the mix of goods, how to produce settles the methods and technology, and for whom to produce settles who the output is meant to serve.
questions.origin: iest1 ch8, 'Key Questions in Economics' and Fig. 8.5, p.188

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: A garment firm that uses more machines and fewer workers is using a method that is:
questions.explanation: Capital-intensive production relies on machines and technology with fewer workers; labour-intensive production does the opposite. The chapter notes the choice depends on the cost of machines, the technology available, the nature of the product, the cost of labour, and government rules.
questions.origin: iest1 ch8, 'How to Produce?', pp.189-190

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: In a planned economy, the major economic decisions are made by:
options: a central planning authority of the government
the forces of demand and supply
private companies competing with each other
questions.explanation: In a planned economy a central planning authority decides what and how much is produced, how, for whom, and at what prices, and the government owns most resources and sectors. Because private enterprise is limited and heavily licensed, competition is weak and there is little pressure to improve quality or innovate.
questions.origin: iest1 ch8, 'Planned Economy', p.191

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which group is given as examples of planned economies?
options: The former Soviet Union, North Korea and Cuba
The United States of America, Japan and Hong Kong
questions.explanation: The chapter names the former Soviet Union, North Korea and Cuba as planned economies. The USA, Japan and Hong Kong are its examples of market economies, while India after 1991, China after 1978, Germany and Sweden are its mixed economies.
questions.origin: iest1 ch8, 'Planned Economy' and 'Market Economy', pp.191-192

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: In a market economy the government is compared to a referee in a football match because it:
options: owns the ground and the players
takes no part in the economy at all
ensures safety and law and order without controlling prices or production
decides which teams may play and what the score should be
questions.explanation: The referee image is about enforcing rules while leaving the play to the players: the state ensures safety and order but does not set prices or output. Note the chapter's qualification - even in market economies the government still plays an important role.
questions.origin: iest1 ch8, 'Market Economy' and Fig. 8.7, p.191

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: India's economy after the reforms of 1991 is best described as:
questions.explanation: After Independence India followed a largely state-led, planned approach. The 1991 reforms cut back regulation, encouraged private enterprise and opened the economy to trade and investment, moving it towards a market orientation while keeping an important role for the government - which is what a mixed economy means.
questions.origin: iest1 ch8, 'Mixed Economy' and the 'Don't Miss Out' box, pp.192-193

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Why does the chapter say that in reality most economies are mixed?
options: Because no country can produce everything it needs
Because private ownership almost always coexists with some degree of government regulation
Because every country has both farms and factories
Because all countries trade with one another
questions.explanation: The defining feature of a mixed economy is that private individuals and enterprises and the government both take part in economic decisions, with private players regulated by the state. On that test even market economies such as the USA and Singapore have significant government involvement.
questions.origin: iest1 ch8, 'Mixed Economy', p.192

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a need rather than a want, as the chapter uses the terms?
questions.explanation: Needs are essentials such as food, water and shelter. Wants are the rest - gadgets, vacations, luxury items - and the chapter notes that they are unlimited and keep changing, as when people move from wanting a bicycle to a motorbike to a car.
questions.origin: iest1 ch8, opening section and Fig. 8.1, p.183

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Economic Survey of India is:
options: an annual document prepared by the Ministry of Finance and presented before the Union Budget
a monthly price index published by the Reserve Bank of India
a census of households conducted every ten years
the government's statement of proposed taxes and spending
questions.explanation: The Economic Survey reviews the past year's performance sector by sector and discusses the challenges ahead, acting as a blueprint for the Budget that follows. The statement of proposed taxes and spending is the Union Budget itself, a separate document.
questions.origin: iest1 ch8, 'Economic Survey: A Report on Indian Economy', p.187

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Assertion: Every economic choice carries an opportunity cost. Reason: Human wants are limited while resources are unlimited.
options: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion
Both are true but the reason does not explain the assertion
The assertion is true but the reason is false
questions.explanation: The assertion is true - choosing one use of a resource means giving up another, and the value of what is given up is the opportunity cost. The reason states the scarcity problem backwards: it is wants that are unlimited and resources that are limited, and it is that way round which forces a choice at all.
questions.origin: iest1 ch8, 'Choices and Limited Resources' and Fig. 8.5, pp.184, 188

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: In economics, demand for a product means:
options: the quantity buyers would like to have, whether or not they can pay
the quantity available in the shops
the quantity a producer plans to make
the quantity buyers are both willing and able to buy at a particular price
questions.explanation: The chapter is careful here: demand is not merely the desire to buy, but desire backed by purchasing power. A person who wants mangoes but cannot pay for them adds nothing to demand. The quantity available for sale is supply, not demand.
questions.origin: iest1 ch9, 'Demand', p.196

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Law of Demand states that, other things remaining the same:
options: quantity demanded does not depend on price
quantity demanded depends only on income
when price rises, quantity demanded falls, and when price falls, quantity demanded rises
when price rises, quantity demanded rises
questions.explanation: The Law of Demand describes an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded, which is why the demand curve slopes downward. Srivalli buys 1 kg of mangoes at 150 rupees, 2 kg at 100 and 3 kg at 50.
questions.origin: iest1 ch9, 'Demand' and Fig. 9.2, p.196

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Market demand is obtained by:
options: adding the individual demands of all buyers at each price
averaging the individual demands of all buyers
taking the demand of the largest single buyer
questions.explanation: Market demand is the sum of individual demands at each price - in the chapter's table, 1 + 2 + 3 kg gives 6 kg at 150 rupees. Because many buyers respond together, the market demand curve is flatter than any one buyer's curve.
questions.origin: iest1 ch9, Table 9.1 and 'Don't Miss Out', pp.197-198

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which pair are complementary goods?
options: An air conditioner and a cooler
questions.explanation: Complementary goods are used together, so demand for one pulls demand for the other along with it - phones and earphones, cars and petrol, printers and cartridges. The other three pairs are substitutes: each can replace the other.
questions.origin: iest1 ch9, 'Price of related goods', p.198

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: If the price of coffee rises while the price of tea stays the same, the demand for tea is likely to:
questions.explanation: Tea and coffee are substitutes. When one becomes dearer, buyers move to the cheaper alternative, so demand for tea rises even though tea's own price has not changed. This is a change caused by the price of a related good, not by the good's own price.
questions.origin: iest1 ch9, 'Price of related goods' - substitute goods, p.198

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The principle of diminishing marginal utility explains why:
options: the additional satisfaction from each extra unit consumed falls, so willingness to pay falls too
