producers supply more when prices rise
market demand curves are flatter than individual ones
questions.explanation: The first mango is delicious, the third much less so. Since each extra unit adds less usefulness than the one before, buyers will pay less for it - which is one reason demand falls as more is consumed. Supply behaviour and sale pricing are separate ideas.
questions.origin: iest1 ch9, 'Think About It' on marginal utility, p.199

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: If consumers expect the price of a durable good to fall during a festival sale, present demand is likely to:
options: stay unchanged, since the current price has not changed
become zero until the sale begins
increase, because people rush to buy now
questions.explanation: Expectations move demand even when today's price has not changed. Expecting a lower price later, buyers wait, and present demand falls; expecting a rise, they buy at once and present demand goes up.
questions.origin: iest1 ch9, 'Future price expectations', p.200

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: The Law of Supply states that as the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied:
questions.explanation: Supply has a direct relationship with price, which is why the supply curve slopes upward - the mirror image of the downward-sloping demand curve. Confusing the two directions is the commonest mistake in this chapter.
questions.origin: iest1 ch9, 'Supply' and Fig. 9.4, p.200

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Why does a higher price lead producers to supply more?
options: Higher prices reduce the cost of raw materials
Higher prices force consumers to buy more
Higher prices are fixed by the government
Higher prices raise profitability, which encourages more output and attracts new firms
questions.explanation: A higher price makes each unit more profitable, so existing producers expand output and new firms are drawn into the market. Nothing about the cost of inputs changes, and buyers respond to higher prices by buying less, not more.
questions.origin: iest1 ch9, 'Supply', p.200

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: How does an improvement in technology, such as drip irrigation, usually affect supply?
options: It changes the price consumers are willing to pay
It lowers the cost of production, so producers can supply more
It raises the cost of production, so supply falls
It has no effect on supply, only on demand
questions.explanation: Better technology brings the cost of producing each unit down, so more can be produced and offered for sale. The chapter's examples are drip irrigation and weather sensors raising crop output, and cold storage letting mangoes reach distant markets.
questions.origin: iest1 ch9, 'Technology' under determinants of supply, p.202

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Market equilibrium is the point at which:
options: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, leaving neither shortage nor surplus
the price is at its lowest possible level
the government fixes the price of the good
questions.explanation: At equilibrium the market is 'cleared': there is no excess demand and no excess supply, so there is no pressure on the price to move. In the chapter's example this happens at 100 rupees, where 12 kg is both demanded and supplied.
questions.origin: iest1 ch9, 'Market Equilibrium', Table 9.3 and Fig. 9.7, pp.203-204

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: If the price is set below the equilibrium price, the market will show:
options: a fall in the quantity demanded
excess demand, that is, a shortage
excess supply, that is, a surplus
questions.explanation: At a low price buyers want much more than sellers are willing to offer, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and a shortage appears - 38 kg wanted against 6 kg supplied at 40 rupees in the chapter's table. A price above equilibrium produces the opposite, a surplus.
questions.origin: iest1 ch9, Table 9.3, p.203

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: A government-fixed maximum price for an essential medicine is an example of a:
questions.explanation: A price ceiling caps how much a seller may charge, and is used to stop overcharging for essentials. A price floor is the opposite - a lower limit, such as a minimum wage, which must be set above the equilibrium price to have any effect.
questions.origin: iest1 ch9, 'Regulation of Unfair Practices' and margin notes, p.206

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Which regulator is named in the chapter as overseeing the securities market?
questions.explanation: The Securities and Exchange Board of India regulates the securities market. The RBI regulates banking, TRAI the telecommunications sector, and the Central Consumer Protection Authority deals with violations of consumer rights and unfair trade practices.
questions.origin: iest1 ch9, 'Don't Miss Out' on regulators, p.206

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: During COVID-19 the government capped the price of sanitisers by declaring them essential commodities under the:
questions.explanation: With demand surging and some shopkeepers hoarding and black-marketing, the government used the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 to cap the maximum retail price at 100 rupees for a 200 ml bottle. As more companies began producing, supply caught up and prices settled.
questions.origin: iest1 ch9, 'Don't Miss Out' on sanitisers, p.207

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.question: Why does the chapter argue that goods such as roads, street lighting and public parks usually have to be provided by the government?
options: People can use them without paying, so private firms cannot make a direct profit from them
Private firms lack the technology to build them
The Constitution forbids private ownership of such goods
They are too cheap for a private firm to bother with
questions.explanation: The chapter's park example makes the point: each family reasons that if others pay, it can use the park anyway, so not enough money is collected and the park is never built. Because nobody can be excluded from using a public good, private provision fails and government funding is needed.
questions.origin: iest1 ch9, 'Provision of Public Goods', p.207
